cells.tense: You are hearing what someone says and what sits under it, right here.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Once this week, act on the first clear thing you hear from someone: say back what you understood, or do the small task it asks, instead of checking it twice.
cells.core:
You can sit with someone and hear what's under the words — the thing they didn't quite get to, the thing in the pause. You ask, you wait, you say the plain thing back, and it's usually right. Company leaves steadier for having been heard this precisely. That's the good version: undefended attention, and almost nobody gives it anymore.
What's free to feed next is movement. You can hear a thing and then do a bit about it rather than filing it away and wondering later whether it landed. Take the next conversation where you understand something clearly, and answer it instead of checking it twice. Put the answer into the same day it arrived. That's what this quiet reading is for.
cells.sheetLine: You can hear what someone means, not only what they said.
cells.verb: listening under the surface of what is said
cells.place: where you keep company with another person

cells.tense: You will keep reading everyone before they have a chance to show you anything.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Choose what you keep trying to read in someone and hold it unknown for a week. Learn a small new fact from them first, and see what you make of it only afterward.
cells.core:
You can read a room before anyone speaks, and lately you read it early — finishing someone's sentence, deciding what a face means, preparing the right response before they reach the point. It will feel like care. From where the other person sits, being understood that fast is lonely; there's nothing left for them to hand you that you haven't already worked out.
So put some motion back. Take what you're carrying about someone close and lean toward it instead of settling it: a deliberate, unhurried move — a real question, a walk together, asking what they'd do — and let surprise be possible. Starting something is how you get surprised again. Build the habit out of that move, not a plan.
cells.sheetLine: Reading people first is not the same as knowing them.

cells.tense: You stopped asking what anyone was really thinking a long time ago.
cells.act: explore the feeling with fresh sensitivity
cells.ask: Sit with what another person's unanswered question stirs in you, five slow minutes, nothing written. Don't finish it, fix it, or decide what they meant.
cells.core:
The deep curiosity used to run — the asking, the not knowing, the willingness to be shown something. In the conversations you have now, the question is finished the same moment it's asked; you answer yourself before it lands, and you don't turn toward the pause or the shift in the mood. Talk ends with the story you came in with. The questions are still there; you're just not turning to them.
Start with something that is no one else's business. Stay with a question someone else would raise and the feeling it brings up in you — five minutes, no filling in an answer, nothing productive done with it. The feeling does the work; you're only staying long enough to let it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped asking because you learned to answer first.
cells.verb: listening under the surface of what is said

cells.tense: You are already keeping things fair between people and calling it nothing.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Put into one sentence how something actually stands between you and someone, without picking a side — what you'd say it is if you had to name it plainly.
cells.core:
You feel the weight of things between people — who gave more, what was fair, where it tipped — and you quietly put your thumb on the honest side. Asked why you stepped in, you shrug it off. And the call is real: you can hold what a thing costs someone next to what it gives them without turning cruel or sentimental.
What's been left to circumstance is that you treat the read as luck. Half of what passes for a feel about a situation isn't chance; it's judgement that you did, and it would be sturdier with a name. When something's off between you and someone, state what you think is fair — once, plainly. If you've been half-stepping to keep the peace, this is the sentence that ends it.
cells.sheetLine: You are already fair, and call it luck.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that any real inward door is closed for the Too Little reader — the record only shows the capacity not arriving, and I have narrowed it to questions that get answered the moment they're asked. A reader could reasonably say their curiosity is alive and it's shame, not absence, that keeps it quiet; the ask holds either way, since carrying one real question is the same act whether the door shut or the person stopped walking through it. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'Every bench holds someone worth understanding' — it is my line about people, not their life, and it comes out of the core.
